messages.author: 5a91d3696b12d600
messages.subject: Stratified sampling with detection clusters
parts: I am estimating a bear population over a large area and we set up a stratified sampling design using trap clusters.  The clusters consist of 5 or so traps about 2000 m apart.  Primary habitat was sampled with clusters 16000 m apart on center and secondary habitat with clusters 25000 m apart on center, meaning that there were fewer clusters in the secondary habitat but the clusters themselves were arranged the same way.  My question is whether I can combine primary and secondary data and analyze as one session.  We had no captures of individuals in more than 1 cluster (no cross-cluster movement).  Since the spacing between traps in a cluster is consistent in both primary and secondary zones, my guess is that density is based wholly on those spacings and the estimates of density in the spaces between clusters should be unbiased.  It would simplify the analysis if I could do it in 1 session but I wanted to check with the group first.  Thanks!  Joe

messages.author: 0dbfcf0efe4ff8fe
messages.subject: Re: Stratified sampling with detection clusters
parts:
Good day,
Just a couple thoughts, if you're asking for reasons to not pool your data into a single session.

I might be concerned that if detection parameters vary between habitat types, then habitat type-specific estimates of density (if of interest) might be biased. Also, since areas of potentially varying detection parameters were not sampled in proportion to their occurrence on the landscape (less intensive sampling in secondary), estimates of average g0, sigma, and D (assuming no spatial variation in any of these parameters) might not be representative of the greater study area.

All the best,

Eric

Your thought about detection probabilities is a good one and we certainly will look at habitat covariates for D, g0 and sigma.  It might be that a multi-session analysis is necessary but what I am asking is whether there is any theoretical reason why they should not be pooled.  This is an already complex analysis over a very wide range and I was trying to simplify things if possible.
Joe

messages.author: 0dbfcf0efe4ff8fe
messages.subject: Re: Stratified sampling with detection clusters
parts:
Hi Joe,

Not sure I follow. If you pool data from different habitat types into a single session, and do not explicitly model spatial variation in detectability or density among (individuals occupying) different habitat types, then estimates of D, g0, and sigma do not all come from data collected within the clusters, they come from the complete data set (regardless of whether any animals are detected at > 1 cluster). In this case, I think, any areas/habitat types sampled more intensively than others will have a disproportionately large influence on parameter estimates.

If you use only habitat type- or cluster-specific data to estimate habitat type-specific or cluster-specific g0, sigma, and D, then I don't see any risk of bias, but estimates might be imprecise. As soon as you combine data without adding parameters to your model, you're entering into the bias-precision trade-off. The theoretical reason to not pool data is to avoid possible bias.

That's not to say sessions are the only solution. A spatial covariate would allow you to avoid assuming constant density in a single-session analysis, and you could model differences in g0 and sigma among individuals in different habitat types using groups. Individual covariates could also be used for detectability, but aren't compatible with a spatial model of D. 

Hopefully others will chime in.


Eric
